lines.text: From the carved stones of a Maya city to banana ports and hurricanes, this is the story of Honduras, a land between two seas.
In 426 a dynasty of Maya kings began to rule at Copan, a city famous for its carved stelae and its great hieroglyphic stairway.
Centuries later, after the Spanish came, the Lenca leader Lempira led the fight against the conquest. The country's money still bears his name.
In 1578 a silver mining town was founded in the hills, Tegucigalpa, which grew to become the capital.
Francisco Morazan, born in 1792, would lead the Federal Republic of Central America and dream of keeping its nations together.
In 1821 Honduras won its independence from Spain, with coasts on both the Caribbean and the Pacific.
By the turn of the century American fruit companies, United Fruit above all, held the north coast, its railways and its ports. Honduras became the first banana republic.
In 1959 Xiomara Castro was born. In 2022 she would become the country's first woman president.
Juan Orlando Hernandez, born in 1968, would be president for eight years, and later be convicted of drug trafficking in the United States.
In 1969, after tense World Cup qualifying matches, Honduras and El Salvador fought a war that lasted about a hundred hours.
In 1998 Hurricane Mitch stalled over Central America, and its floods and landslides killed about eleven thousand people, many of them in Honduras.
And in 2009 the army removed President Manuel Zelaya, flying him out of the country, in a coup that divided the nation.
Through storms and upheaval, Honduras carries on, still shaped by Copan, the banana coast and its people.
